STRESSEVAL: Failure-Driven Dynamic Benchmarking for Knowledge-Intensive
Reasoning in Large Language Models
Yongrui Chen1 , Yangyang Ma1 , Xiaoying Huang4 , Shenyu Zhang1 ,
Huajun Chen2 , Haofen Wang3 and Guilin Qi1,∗
1Southeast University
2Zhejiang University

{yongruichen, gqi}@seu.edu.cn.com
Abstract
Static benchmarks for LLMs are increasingly com-
1
promised by contamination and overfitting, es-
2
pecially on knowledge-intensive reasoning tasks.
3
While recent dynamic benchmarks can alleviate
4
staleness, they often increase difficulty at the ex-
5
pense of answerability and controllability.
In
6
this paper, we propose STRESSEVAL, a failure-
7
driven data synthesis framework that turns ob-
8
served model failures into dynamic, challenging,
9
and controlable test instances. STRESSEVAL con-
10
sists of three stages:
(i) it constructs a semi-
11
structured difficulty card that identifies the failed
12
reasoning step and its root cause; (ii) it applies
13
a dual-perspective instance-synthesis method that
14
targets both knowledge gaps and reasoning break-
15
downs while preserving the underlying difficulty
16
factors; and (iii) it applies a gating mechanism
17
to retain only grounded, unambiguous instances.
18
Seeding from multiple knowledge-intensive rea-
19
soning datasets, we employ STRESSEVAL to build
20
DYNAMIC-ONEEVAL1, a focused suite of chal-
21
lenging dynamic benchmark. Across several state-
22
of-the-art LLMs, DYNAMIC-ONEEVAL yields sub-
23
stantially larger performance drops than the orig-
24
inal benchmarks while retaining explicit difficulty
25
factors, enabling more actionable iteration.
26
1
Introduction
27
Large language models (LLMs) have advanced rapidly, de-
28
livering strong performance across a broad range of language
29
understanding tasks and increasingly sophisticated forms
30
of reasoning [Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI, 2023].
How-
31
ever, as model architectures and training pipelines evolve at
32
pace, conventional static evaluation paradigms [Chen, 2021;
33
Hendrycks et al., 2021; Yue et al., 2024] are becoming less
34
informative. Leaderboard gains can obscure brittle behav-
35
iors, while widespread benchmark reuse and dataset con-
36
tamination make it difficult to disentangle genuine general-
37
ization from memorization or overfitting [Lin et al., 2024b;

39
These limitations are especially pronounced for knowledge-
40
intensive reasoning like ONEEVAL [Chen et al., 2025b],
41
where success hinges on up-to-date factual knowledge, care-
42
ful grounding, and reliable multi-step inference [Jiang et al.,
43
2024; Zhou et al., 2025].
44
Recent work [White et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025] has
45
begun to explore dynamic benchmarks that leverage auto-
46
matic data synthesis to keep evaluations continually refreshed
47
and more resistant to benchmark contamination [White et
48
al., 2024; Li et al., 2024]. While this direction can miti-
49
gate staleness, automatically generated instances often drift
50
toward ungrounded content or superficially adversarial tricks,
51
rather than isolating a well-defined capability or failure
52
mode [White et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025]
53
(see the bottom-left of Figure 1). Consequently, the revealed
54
errors are difficult to interpret and even harder to translate
55
into actionable mitigations for model designers. This raises
56
an open problem: how to generate evaluation instances that
57
are both (i) challenging: they reliably stress specific knowl-
58
edge points or reasoning patterns where models are weak, and
59
(ii) controllable difficulty: their construction is governed by
60
explicit factors so that failures can be traced back to concrete
61
causes and directly guide model or system improvements.
62
To address this gap, we propose STRESSEVAL, a failure-
63
driven data synthesis framework. Rather than generating dif-
64

ficulty from scratch, STRESSEVAL uses a three-stage pipeline
65
that turns model’s failure cases into follow-up instances
66
that remain answerable and controlable, while systematically
67
stressing the same underlying weakness (see the right of Fig-
68
ure 1).
First, Structured Error Analysis takes instances
69
where a model produces incorrect responses as input and em-
70
ploys an LLM-based analyzer to reconstruct the model’s rea-
71
soning trajectory, pinpoint the bottleneck step, and diagnose
72
the underlying root cause. It outputs a semi-structured diffi-
73
culty card that records both the failing reasoning step and the
74
triggering input property. Second, guided by the difficulty
75
card, Dual-Perspective Instance Synthesis leverages LLMs
76
to generate new challenges from two complementary per-
77
spectives: for knowledge stress, it freezes the original knowl-
78
edge source, canonicalizes the missing fact as an atomic
79
knowledge black box, and synthesizes dependency-aware
80
questions and answers that still hinge on that missing fact; for
81
reasoning stress, it synthesizes a fictitious but internally con-
82
sistent virtual knowledge source with synthetic entities and
83
then generates new question-answer pairs via a reasoning-
84
skeleton procedure that inherits the same bottleneck and trig-
85
ger while keeping the answer uniquely grounded. Third, a
86
Multi-criteria Gating mechanism applies two LLM-based
87
screening schemes, retaining only grounded instances that
88
preserve the targeted difficulty card. We seed STRESSEVAL
89
with multiple knowledge-intensive reasoning datasets and use
90
it to produce a focused suite of high-difficulty evaluation
91
items, STRESSEVAL-BENCH. Compared to the seed bench-
92
marks, STRESSEVAL-BENCH yields substantially larger per-
93
formance degradations across several state-of-the-art LLMs,
94
while preserving explicit grounding and controllable diffi-
95
culty factors. In summary, our contributions include:
96
• We propose STRESSEVAL, the first failure-driven frame-
97
work for benchmarking knowledge-intensive reasoning
98
that systematically converts observed model failures into
99
new, difficulty-controllable test instances.
100
• We propose a complementary dual-perspective instance-
101
synthesis method that systematically targets LLMs’
102
knowledge gaps and reasoning breakdowns, enabling
103
faithful reconstruction of specific difficulty factors.
104
• Comprehensive experiments on our released dynamic
105
DYNAMIC-ONEEVAL demonstrate its difficulty and
106
quality, and reveal that even state-of-the-art LLMs ex-
107
hibit pronounced weaknesses in knowledge-intensive
108
reasoning as well as fine-grained failure modes.
109
2
Problem Formulation
110
Assume a seed dataset Ω= {(Qi, Si, Ai)}N
i=1, where Qi is
111
a question, Si is its associated knowledge source (e.g., un-
112
structured documents, semi-structured tables, or structured
113
knowledge graphs), and Ai is the gold answer. We evalu-
114
ate an LLM M on Ωand collect the instances on which it
115
produces incorrect predictions. This yields a set of failure
116
cases E = {(Qi, Si, Ai, Yi)}M
i=1, where Yi denotes the model
117
output and M is the number of errors. Crucially, the source
118
context S may be incomplete, i.e., it may not contain all in-
119
formation required to answer Q, reflecting realistic retrieval-
120
augmented generation settings in which models must reason
121
under partial evidence.
122
Our objective is to leverage E to automatically construct a
123
new dataset Ω∗= {(Q∗
k, S∗
k, A∗
k)}K
k=1, where each synthe-
124
sized instance is derived from one failure cases and explicitly
125
preserves the key difficulty factors that caused M to fail (e.g.,
126
missing or partial fact in S, multi-hop reasoning, composi-
127
tional constraints, or distractors). The resulting dataset Ω′ is
128
designed to be challenging for the model M.
129
3
STRESSEVAL
130
Figure 2 shows the overview of our proposed STRESSEVAL
131
framework, which consists of: (i) Structured Error Analy-
132
sis localizes the broken reasoning step and attributes the fail-
133
ure to a root cause; (ii) Dual-Perspective Instance Synthe-
134
sis generates new challenging instances from the perspectives
135
of knowledge stress and reasoning stress; and (iii) Multi-
136
criterion Gating uses two LLM reviewers to enforce quality
137
controls, retaining only instances that are well-grounded, and
138
that instantiate the intended difficulty.
139
3.1
Structured Error Analysis
140
For each failure case ei = (Qi, Si, Ai, Yi) ∈E, we use
141
an LLM as an analyzer to generate a structured error report.
142
Concretely, let fana denote a reasoning LLM and Pana be an
143
analysis prompt template. We obtain
144
(γi, Ψi) ∼pfana(· | Pana(Qi, Si, Ai, Yi)) ,
(1)
where γi ∈Γ is a root-cause label that characterizes the
145
error type with a concise, precise phrase (e.g., Entity
146
Linking Confusion), and Ψi is our difficulty card that
147
summarizes the primary challenge underlying the failure.
148
Difficulty card.
Our defined Ψi aims to make each ei ∈E
149
both interpretable (clarifying why it is difficult) and control-
150
lable (specifying how to preserve the same difficulty). It com-
151
prises the following fixed slots: (i) Bottleneck Step: the rea-
152
soning stage where the model fails (e.g., entity/relation recog-
153
nition or comparison). For example, in the lower-left cor-
154
ner of Figure 2, for the question Which plan is cheaper per
155
month?, the model breaks at unit-time normalization due to
156
misinterpreting the term field in the table. (ii) Trigger: the in-
157
put property, described in natural language, that triggers the
158
failure. In the running example, mixed billing terms (monthly
159
vs. yearly) create a unit mismatch that the model does not rec-
160
oncile, causing it to compare prices without converting them
161
to a common time basis (e.g., per month).
162
3.2
Dual-Perspective Instance Synthesis
163
Unlike existing methods [Lin et al., 2024a; Zhao et al., 2025;
164
Wang et al., 2025], we observe that failure-driven instance
165
synthesis is prone to root-cause entanglement: without an ex-
166
plicit separation of failure sources, a synthesized instance can
167
inadvertently mix missing-fact and reasoning breakdowns,
168
causing the stress type to be mislabeled or the difficulty to
169
drift (e.g., becoming trivial or unanswerable). This reduces
170
controllability and weakens coverage of failure modes.
171
To address this, we partition the observed failure cases E
172
into two complementary perspectives according to the root-
173
cause label γi and difficulty card:

179
• Reasoning-stress (Γr) failures: instances in which the
180
provided knowledge source Si contains sufficient infor-
181
mation to answer correctly, yet the model still produces
182

183

184
Below, we will introduce how to synthesize new, high-quality,
185
and challenging test instances from each perspective.
186
Knowledge-stress Instance Synthesis
187
This branch aims to preserve the knowledge stress by freez-
188
ing the original knowledge context Si. Intuitively, since the
189
model answered question Qi incorrectly due to missing fact,
190
it is reasonable to expect that it will also answer incorrectly
191
any questions derived from Qi. Specifically, for any failure
192
case ei with γi ∈Γk, we keep: S∗
i := Si.
193
Knowledge black box.
For knowledge-stress failures, the
194
missing fact is external to the provided source Si, so a faith-
195
ful step-by-step decomposition is often underspecified: the
196
model fails not because of an explicit reasoning error over
197
Si, but because a crucial fact is unavailable. To preserve this
198
knowledge gap while enabling controlled synthesis, we col-
199
lapse the original question–answer pair into a self-contained
200
atomic knowledge statement (like black box), denoted as K0,
201
and treat it as an indivisible unit that can be re-queried or
202
rephrased without altering the underlying missing fact:
203
K0 ∼pLcan(· | Pcan(Qi, Ai)) ,
(2)
where Lcan is an reasoning LLM used for canonicalization
204
(with prompt template Pcan), and Pcan is a prompt tem-
205

206
contained knowledge statement. For instance, from Qi: What
207
is the maximum channel bandwidth supported by Wi-Fi 7?
208
and Ai: 320 MHz, we obtain canonical Ki: The maximum
209
channel bandwidth supported by Wi-Fi 7 is 320 MHz.

Then, we extract a new,
211
definitive piece of knowledge ∆K from Si (i.e., directly
212
supported by Si and thus reliable), and combine it with

faithful to the fixed source S∗

solving it still hinges on first resolving the original Qi.

Reasoning-stress Instance Synthesis
224
This branch aims to reproduce the same reasoning trap in new
225
instances that are fully answerable from the provided con-
226
text. For any failure case ei with γi ∈Γr, we create a virtual
227
knowledge source with fictitious entities to prevent the model
228
from exploiting parametric memory.
229
Virtual knowledge source synthesis.
We first employ an
230
LLM to sample a synthetic universe
231
Ui = (E, R, V) ∼pfU (· | PU(Qi, Si, Ai, Ψi)) ,
(5)

(6)

237

238

Given the

virtual Sr

241
question-answer pair while explicitly inheriting the original
242
reasoning bottleneck and trigger. Here, we use a two-step
243
LLM procedure: (i) generate a reasoning skeleton that oper-
244

245
operations and a concrete trap injection (e.g., an ambigui-
246
ty/distractor that targets the bottleneck step), and (ii) render
247
the skeleton into a natural-language question whose gold an-
248
swer is uniquely derivable from S∗
i .

3.3
Multi-criterion Gating
264
In this stage, we perform multi-criterion gating to control the
265
quality of synthesized instances. For each candidate instance
266
xi = (Si, Qi, Ai, Ψi), we query two LLM-based reviewers,
267
each prompted to return a structured verdict together with a
268
calibrated confidence score. Specifically, we use: (1) an An-
269
swerability reviewer, which verifies that the question is an-
270
swerable under the intended stress type and that the gold an-
271
swer is properly grounded—i.e., supported by explicit span-
272
s/records in Si for reasoning-stress, or demonstrably requir-
273

274
and (2) a Consistency reviewer, which attempts to solve the
275
instance, checks internal consistency among Si, Qi, Ai, and
276
verifies that the difficulty card Ψi is actually instantiated
277
rather than merely stated.
278
Each reviewer outputs a binary decision with confidence.
279

4.1
Seed Data & Implementation Details
289
To initialize DYNAMIC-ONEEVAL, we draw seed instances
290
from widely used benchmarks.
a) Text Reasoning: Hot-
291

tiple documents to answer.
b) KG Reasoning:
Com-

295

301
We generated seed failure cases E by prompting GPT-
302

303

304

305
to-end quality control, the strong GPT-5.2 model was used
306

fU, fU. All API calls used deterministic decoding with tem-

309

310
sEval will synthesize 5 ∼10 instances. In addition, we do
311

312

313

314

346
We conducted a lightweight human evaluation to assess the
347
quality of DYNAMIC-ONEEVAL. We randomly sampled 50
348

349
stress Γr, covering diverse root-cause labels γ ∈Γ, and
350

351
mensions. First, answerability (A) evaluates whether the in-
352

353
whether the gold answer A is supported by explicit context
354
in S; for Γk, whether solving the question Q necessarily re-
355
quires an external fact missing from S. Second, unambigu-
356
ity (U) assesses whether a unique gold answer exists. Third,
357
faithfulness to difficulty cards (F) measures whether the diffi-
358
culty card Ψ is correctly instantiated, meaning that the speci-
359
fied bottleneck step and trigger are present in the instance.

The results are reported in the right panel of Table 1. Over-
361
all, human judgments show consistently high A and U across
362
splits, indicating that instances are generally solvable from
363
the provided context and admit a unique gold answer. In con-
364

365

366

367

368

fact or ambiguity. Aggregated over the benchmark, the strong
370

Ablation Studies
415
We fix GPT-5.2 as the synthesis backbone, generate in-
416
stances under each ablated setting, and evaluate the resulting
417
datasets using DeepSeek V3.2, together with human judg-
418

Here, we consider
419
three ablation groups. Pipeline-level ablations remove ei-
420
ther (a) error analysis, to test whether bottleneck identifi-
421
cation and trigger localization are necessary for controllable
422
synthesis, or (b) criterion gating, to quantify its role in en-
423
forcing grounding, answerability, unambiguity, and difficulty
424
preservation. Knowledge-stress ablations remove either (c)
425
the missing-fact black box ∆K, to test whether explicitly
426
modeling atomic missing facts stabilizes reliance on exter-
427
nal knowledge, or (d) context freezing, allowing S to be
428
rewritten and potentially filling the intended knowledge gap.
429
Reasoning-stress ablations remove either (e) virtual con-
430
text S∗construction, to assess whether entity virtualization
431
prevents parametric-memory shortcuts, or (f) the reasoning
432
skeleton, to test whether explicitly instantiating the bottleneck
433
and injecting traps improves faithfulness and grounding.

gap, consistent with context leakage. For R-stress, remov-

Related Work
480
Knowledge-Intensive Reasoning Benchmarks
Early suc-
481
cess of LLMs, exemplified by models like GPT-4 [OpenAI,
482
2023] and DeepSeek [Liu et al., 2024], demonstrated impres-
483
sive capabilities across a spectrum of language understanding
484
and reasoning tasks. However, conventional static evaluation
485
practices have struggled to keep pace with the rapid evolu-
486
tion of these models. Issues such as benchmark contamina-
487
tion [Deng et al., 2024; Dong et al., ], where models may
488
memorize test data present in their vast training corpora, lead
489
to an inflated sense of performance and obscure genuine gen-
490
eralization abilities [Lin et al., 2024b]. This problem is par-
491
ticularly acute in knowledge-intensive settings [Chen et al.,
492
2025a; Chen et al., 2022], where correctness relies on up-to-
493
date facts, strict grounding, and robust multi-step inference,
494
rather than superficial pattern matching [Jiang et al., 2024].
495
The need for benchmarks that can genuinely assess an LLM’s
496
ability to reason with and apply external knowledge, rather
497
than merely recall memorized patterns, remains a significant
498
challenge. Our work directly addresses this by creating in-
499
stances that expose specific knowledge gaps and reasoning
500
failures that are otherwise masked by existing benchmarks.
501
Dynamic LLM Benchmarks
Prior efforts in automatic
502
benchmarking [Wang et al., 2025] broadly fall into four cate-
503
gories: (i) static, human-curated benchmark suites; (ii) LLM-
504
as-judge evaluation frameworks such as MT-Bench [Zheng
505
et al., 2023]; (iii) agent-driven, end-to-end automated arenas
506
(e.g., Auto-Arena [Zhao et al., 2025]); and (iv) in-the-wild ro-
507
bustness benchmarks mined from real user interactions, such
508
as WildBench [Lin et al., 2024a]. These approaches improve
509
scalability and realism but have complementary drawbacks:
510
static benchmarks saturate, risk data contamination, and of-
511
fer limited diagnostics; mined in-the-wild sets reveal real
512
failures but lack controllable latent factors for causal stress
513
tests [Valiulla, 2025]; and fully automated agent pipelines
514
boost throughput and ranking but may generate cases that
515
are not reliably answerable, controlable, or causally faith-
516
ful—limiting debugging and improvement [Shukla, 2025].
517
Model-in-the-loop, continual, and adversarial test-generation
518
frameworks aim to keep evaluations up to date and to un-
519
cover brittle heuristics that static benchmarks can miss [White
520
et al., 2024; Li et al., 2024].
However, without strict
521
constraints on answerability and provenance, such dynamic
522
generation can drift toward unanswerable, underspecified,
523
or spurious examples, weakening both the validity and the
524
actionability of the resulting evaluations [Li et al., 2024;
525
White et al., 2024]. Compared with these benchmarks, our
526
STRESSEVAL prioritizes causal attribution, difficulty preser-
527
vation, contamination resistance.
528
7
Conclusion
529
We present STRESSEVAL, a failure-driven pipeline that con-
530
verts observed LLM failures into dynamic, answerable, and
531
high-difficulty evaluation instances through structured er-
532
ror analysis, dual-perspective instance synthesis, and multi-
533

criterion gating. Instantiated from knowledge-intensive seed
534
datasets, STRESSEVAL produces grounded and controlable
535
tests that induce substantially larger, and more diagnostic,
536
performance drops across frontier models than standard static
537
benchmarks, while preserving explicit difficulty factors to
538
support actionable iteration. Future work will investigate how
539
different combinations of LLMs within the same STRESSE-
540
VAL framework affect data generation, e.g., using heteroge-
541
neous generator–critic–verifier ensembles, to improve diver-
542
sity, robustness, and controllability.
